listening.title: Students blast off to US for Nasa robotics competition
listening.topic: A team of engineering students from Queen's University Belfast is competing in NASA's Lunabotics competition in Florida, where they will test a robot designed for future lunar missions.
listening.topic_zh: 北愛爾蘭貝爾法斯特女王大學的工程學生團隊將赴佛羅里達參加NASA月球機器人競賽，測試他們為未來月球任務設計的機器人。
listening.transcript_excerpt: Space exploration has long captured the imagination of engineers and scientists alike, but increasingly it is university students who are pushing the boundaries of what is possible. A prime example of this trend is a team of ten engineering students from Queen's University Belfast, who have earned their place in NASA's prestigious Lunabotics competition, held at the University of Central Florida. The competition challenges university teams from around the world to design, build, and operate a robot capable of performing tasks on the lunar surface. These tasks include excavating lunar material, navigating over physical obstacles, and using that material to construct a protective wall — all skills that would be essential for establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon. The QUB team divided their responsibilities into three specialist groups: software, electronics, and mechanical engineering. Jamie Smith, the software team lead and a third-year electrical engineering student, explained that his group's primary challenge was developing the autonomous capabilities of the rover — essentially teaching it to make decisions independently. Meanwhile, PhD student Jack Fitzpatrick and the mechanical team focused on ensuring the robot could withstand the physical demands of lunar terrain. What makes this achievement particularly impressive is that the students had to simulate the robot's behaviour in virtual environments before a physical prototype was even available. Their qualification for the Florida competition followed a victory in an earlier round, demonstrating both their technical expertise and their determination to compete on the world stage.

reading.title: Student-Led Robotics and the Future of Lunar Exploration
reading.passage:
The involvement of university students in space exploration has grown significantly in recent decades, with organisations such as NASA actively cultivating the next generation of aerospace engineers through competitive programmes. Among the most prominent of these is the Lunabotics competition, an annual event that challenges student teams from universities worldwide to design, construct, and operate a robotic system capable of functioning on the lunar surface. Participating teams must adhere to NASA's systems engineering process — a disciplined, iterative methodology that mirrors the practices used in professional aerospace development.

The competition tasks are deliberately designed to reflect the genuine challenges of lunar exploration. Robots must demonstrate the capacity to excavate regolith, the loose fragmented material covering the Moon's surface, navigate unpredictable terrain, and utilise extracted material to erect basic structures. These requirements are directly informed by NASA's long-term ambitions to establish a sustainable human presence on the Moon, where locally sourced materials would be essential for building habitats and infrastructure without the prohibitive cost of transporting supplies from Earth.

One competing team, from Queen's University Belfast in Northern Ireland, exemplifies the multidisciplinary nature of such endeavours. Their ten-member group was structured into software, electronics, and mechanical sub-teams, each contributing specialised expertise to a unified project. A particularly noteworthy aspect of their preparation was the development of virtual simulations that allowed the software team to validate their algorithms and autonomous control systems before a physical prototype was available. This approach — building digital twins prior to hardware construction — is increasingly standard in professional engineering contexts and reflects the pedagogical value of competition-based learning.

Such competitions serve a dual purpose: they accelerate technological innovation while simultaneously preparing students for careers in industries where interdisciplinary collaboration and iterative problem-solving are paramount. As space agencies worldwide intensify their lunar programmes, the pipeline of talent being developed through initiatives like Lunabotics will likely prove indispensable to humanity's broader ambitions beyond Earth.

questions.statement: NASA's Lunabotics competition is open to professional engineering firms as well as university teams.
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that Lunabotics is a university-level competition for student teams. No mention is made of professional firms participating; in fact, the context emphasises student and academic involvement throughout.

questions.statement: The robots in the Lunabotics competition are required to use excavated lunar material to construct structures.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that robots must utilise extracted material to erect basic structures, directly confirming this statement as true.

questions.statement: The Queen's University Belfast team consisted of students exclusively from the mechanical engineering department.
questions.explanation: The passage states the team included students across software, electronics, and mechanical sub-teams, indicating a multidisciplinary composition rather than a single-department group.

questions.q: According to the passage, why would locally sourced lunar materials be particularly valuable for future Moon missions?
options: A: They are lighter than materials transported from Earth
B: They eliminate the need for human astronauts on the surface
C: They would reduce the excessive cost of transporting supplies from Earth
D: They have been proven to be structurally superior to man-made materials
questions.explanation: The passage states that locally sourced materials would be essential for building habitats and infrastructure 'without the prohibitive cost of transporting supplies from Earth', making option C the correct answer. No other options are supported by the text.

speaking.topic: Describe a time when you worked as part of a team to achieve a challenging goal
speaking.topic_zh: 描述一次你作為團隊一員共同完成具有挑戰性目標的經歷

part2.cue_card:
Describe a time when you worked as part of a team to achieve a challenging goal.

You should say:
• what the goal or project was
• who was involved in the team and what roles people played
• what difficulties or obstacles the team encountered
• and explain how you felt about the experience and what you learned from it.

You will have one minute to prepare. Then speak for one to two minutes.
band_tips: Use a range of narrative tenses naturally — past simple, past continuous, and past perfect — to show grammatical sophistication when recounting the sequence of events and challenges your team faced.

Incorporate topic-specific vocabulary related to collaboration, problem-solving, and achievement such as 'coordinate responsibilities', 'leverage individual strengths', 'iterative process', and 'collective effort' to demonstrate lexical range appropriate for Band 7-9.

Develop your answer beyond a simple description by reflecting on what the experience revealed about teamwork dynamics, leadership, or your own capabilities — examiners reward depth of thought and the ability to move from concrete examples to abstract insights.

part3.q: Do you think universities should place more emphasis on teamwork and collaborative projects rather than individual academic assessments?
part3.q_zh: 你認為大學應該更注重團隊合作和協作項目，而非個人學術評估嗎？
key_points: Collaborative projects better mirror real-world professional environments where interdisciplinary teamwork is the norm, particularly in fields like engineering, medicine, and business
However, individual assessments remain important for accurately measuring each student's personal understanding and preventing free-riding, where weaker contributors benefit from others' efforts
A balanced approach — combining both modes of assessment — would arguably develop well-rounded graduates who are both independently competent and effective collaborators

part3.q: How has technology changed the way people collaborate on complex projects in the modern workplace?
part3.q_zh: 科技如何改變現代職場中人們在複雜項目上的協作方式？
key_points: Digital tools such as cloud-based platforms, project management software, and real-time communication applications have made it possible for geographically dispersed teams to collaborate seamlessly across time zones

Virtual simulations and digital prototyping — as demonstrated by the NASA robotics students — allow teams to test concepts and identify problems far earlier in the development process, saving time and resources

However, over-reliance on digital communication can reduce the quality of interpersonal relationships within teams, potentially undermining trust and the kind of spontaneous creativity that emerges from face-to-face interaction

part3.q: To what extent do you think international competitions like NASA's Lunabotics inspire young people to pursue careers in science and technology?
part3.q_zh: 你認為像NASA月球機器人這樣的國際競賽在多大程度上激勵年輕人追求科學和技術職業？
key_points: High-profile competitions generate significant media coverage and public excitement, making STEM careers appear dynamic, creative, and globally significant to younger audiences who might otherwise perceive them as inaccessible or abstract

The competitive format instils intrinsic motivation by giving students tangible goals, real-world stakes, and the opportunity to benchmark their abilities against international peers — a powerful complement to traditional academic study

Nevertheless, the inspirational effect may be limited if young people from disadvantaged backgrounds lack access to the resources, mentorship, and institutional support needed to participate in such competitions in the first place

part3.q: Some people argue that the money invested in space exploration would be better spent addressing problems on Earth. Do you agree or disagree?
part3.q_zh: 有些人認為投資太空探索的資金最好用於解決地球上的問題。你同意還是不同意？
key_points: Space research has historically generated significant technological spin-offs — including satellite navigation, water purification technology, and medical imaging advances — that directly benefit everyday life on Earth, suggesting the dichotomy between space investment and earthly benefit is somewhat false

From an ethical standpoint, it is reasonable to question whether billions spent on lunar missions are justifiable while millions of people lack access to clean water, adequate healthcare, or climate change mitigation

A nuanced position might argue that modest, strategically targeted space investment is worthwhile given its long-term returns, but that unchecked expansion of space budgets during periods of acute global crisis requires careful democratic scrutiny

writing.task2_question: Some people believe that governments should invest heavily in space exploration and robotics technology, as these fields will ultimately benefit all of humanity. Others argue that such investment is wasteful when urgent problems on Earth remain unsolved. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
writing.task2_question_zh: 一些人認為政府應該大力投資太空探索和機器人技術，因為這些領域最終將使全人類受益。另一些人則認為，當地球上緊迫的問題尚未解決時，這樣的投資是一種浪費。討論兩種觀點並給出你自己的意見。

useful_phrases.phrase: proponents of this view contend that
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when introducing the arguments of one side in a discussion essay, particularly to attribute a position clearly before developing it
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 在討論型文章中介紹某一方觀點時使用，用於清晰地歸因立場再進行展開
useful_phrases.example: Proponents of this view contend that investment in robotics and space technology generates technological breakthroughs whose benefits eventually permeate every sector of society.

useful_phrases.phrase: it would be shortsighted to overlook the fact that
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when conceding a point made by the opposing side while steering the argument back towards your own position
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 在承認對立方觀點後，將論述導回自身立場時使用，適合表達讓步與反駁的轉折
useful_phrases.example: It would be shortsighted to overlook the fact that many of today's most essential technologies — from GPS to weather forecasting — are direct products of space research.

useful_phrases.phrase: a more nuanced perspective would suggest that
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when moving beyond a binary either-or argument to propose a more sophisticated, balanced position, particularly in the conclusion or thesis statement
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於超越非此即彼的二元論述，提出更精緻平衡的立場，適合用在論點陳述或結論段落
useful_phrases.example: A more nuanced perspective would suggest that the question is not whether to fund space exploration, but rather how to ensure such funding is proportionate and strategically justified.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when discussing consequences or implications that extend well into the future, lending an analytical and forward-looking tone to your argument
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 討論深遠的未來影響時使用，為論述增添分析性和前瞻性的語氣
useful_phrases.example: The long-term ramifications of neglecting investment in space technology could leave nations ill-equipped for the geopolitical and scientific challenges of the coming century.

useful_phrases.phrase: it is incumbent upon policymakers to strike a balance between
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use in conclusions or body paragraphs that argue for a middle-ground solution, particularly in problem-solution or discussion essays addressing government responsibility
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 在結論或主體段落中主張折衷方案時使用，尤其適用於涉及政府責任的問題解決型或討論型文章
useful_phrases.example: It is incumbent upon policymakers to strike a balance between ambitious investment in future-oriented technologies and the immediate moral obligation to address poverty and climate change.

outline.intro: Begin by paraphrasing the prompt to establish the debate between the visionary case for space and robotics investment and the pragmatic argument that earthly crises demand priority. Present a clear thesis that acknowledges the legitimacy of both perspectives while indicating a qualified position — for example, that strategic, proportionate investment in space technology is justifiable given its demonstrable long-term benefits, provided it does not come at the direct expense of critical social programmes.
outline.body1: Develop the case in favour of space and robotics investment. Argue that history demonstrates how such research generates transformative technological spin-offs that benefit society broadly — satellite communications, medical imaging, and advanced materials all have roots in space programmes. Use the NASA Lunabotics competition as a contextual example to illustrate how such investment also cultivates a skilled engineering workforce, fostering innovation that extends far beyond space itself. Acknowledge that these benefits may take decades to materialise fully.
outline.body2: Present and engage with the opposing view — that governments have a more pressing moral obligation to direct funding towards poverty alleviation, healthcare, climate change mitigation, and education. Concede that this argument carries genuine ethical weight, particularly in developing nations where basic needs remain unmet. However, challenge the premise that space investment and social spending are mutually exclusive, arguing that the framing of a binary choice is misleading, and that well-governed economies can pursue both priorities simultaneously without one necessarily diminishing the other.
outline.conclusion: Restate your balanced thesis, affirming that space exploration and robotics represent a legitimate and strategically important investment for humanity's long-term future, but that this investment must be proportionate, transparent, and pursued alongside — not instead of — efforts to address immediate human needs. End with a forward-looking sentence that connects technological ambition with broader human values.
